title: The Grike's Arithmetic
summary: A short poem on the Burren's limestone pavement — the crack, not the stone, is where everything actually grows.
content:
Nothing here agreed to grow easy.
The pavement cracked once, long before us,
and every root since has taken the crack's side —
not the stone's.

Call it soil if you like. It is mostly absence:
a finger's width of dark between two grey slabs,
enough for a gentian to call home,
enough for a fern to call deep enough.

The arithmetic is simple and merciless —
less ground than anywhere, more flower than anywhere,
and no one has explained that trade
except the grike itself, which keeps no ledger,
only the crack, only the blue.

title: Poulnabrone
summary: A short elegy at the portal tomb — five thousand years and the capstone still holds its angle.
content:
Five thousand years and the stone still holds its angle,
capstone tilted like a held breath,
like something about to be said
and thinking better of it.

They buried the dead here standing almost,
knees drawn up, facing whatever direction
faces mattered in — we don't ask the stone,
it wouldn't answer the way we'd want.

What's left is the shape of a decision:
two uprights, one weight balanced between them,
a door built for no one to walk through,
only to walk past, and slow down.

title: Compline at Corcomroe
summary: A short devotional poem at the ruined abbey, where swallows have taken over the evening office.
content:
The roof gave up centuries ago
and the monks with it, but the walls kept
the shape of an hour they used to keep —
last light, last office, last word before sleep.

Now it's swallows that take the evening watch,
stitching the empty window with their going,
and the carved stone faces overhead
still listening for something sung.

Stand here at the right hour
and the valley does the singing for them —
wind through the east window,
a psalm with no one left to close it.

title: Cliff Notation
summary: A short coastal poem at the Cliffs of Moher, on scale, patience, and an ocean still mid-sentence.
content:
Two hundred metres is not a number
until you're the one standing at the top of it,
watching gannets fold their wings at the exact moment
faith requires and gravity permits.

The Atlantic doesn't perform for anyone.
It was doing this before there were cliffs to hit,
and it will keep doing it after,
patient the way only erosion is patient.

Every guidebook calls this a view.
Standing here, it is closer to a sentence
the ocean has been writing for six thousand years,
and hasn't reached the end of yet.

title: Doolin, Low Tide
summary: A short portrait of Doolin with the tide out, the currachs beached, and a fiddle tune drifting from a doorway.
content:
The tide goes out far enough here
to make liars of the maps,
flat rock where there should be water,
a fiddle tune drifting down from the pub door
like it's not sure the sea is really gone.

Someone's currach is up on the stones,
someone's washing is up on the line,
and the whole town holds still for an hour,
the way a place does
when it knows the water is only resting.

By dark it will all come back —
the tide, the boats, the noise from the doorway —
but for now: bare rock, bare sky,
and a town that knows exactly
how long low tide lasts.
